extraction.name: MATHVISTA
extraction.description: A benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in visual contexts, consisting of 6,141 examples derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets and 3 newly created datasets.
extraction.creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was compiled by collecting 9 multimodal MathQA datasets, reviewing more than 70 VQA datasets and selecting 19 publicly available math-related ones using heuristic rules plus manual labeling, and creating 3 new datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA) with manual annotation and review.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Only 85.6% of examples have annotations because annotations were sourced from original data providers and sources were heterogeneous.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data came from 31 source datasets: 28 existing multimodal datasets and 3 newly created datasets; IQTest was sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms, and PaperQA used academic illustrations from online education resources with 107 examples sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For VQA datasets, heuristic rules automatically selected likely math-related examples by choosing examples with numeric answers or quantity words; source datasets were capped at 400 examples; the benchmark was split into testmini and test using random sampling to preserve source distribution; several quality checks were conducted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three expert annotators manually labeled filtered VQA examples to determine whether they involved mathematical reasoning. For the three new datasets, questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and refined through a two-step review process with three reviewers per dataset. Metadata such as question type, answer type, language, source, category, task, grade level, and visual context were annotated from source dataset details, and expert annotators manually labeled mathematical reasoning categories for 1,000 examples to verify automatic annotation quality.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Majority voting was used for VQA math-related labeling; disagreements in new dataset annotations were resolved through team discussion; inter-annotator consistency for new datasets was 99.2% with only 6 disagreements among 736 questions; Fleiss Kappa for mathematical reasoning labeling was 0.775; automatic reasoning-type annotation matched human labels on 94.1% of examples and 98.79% of individual labels.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Graduate students in STEM fields; expert annotators; qualified human annotators with a high school diploma or higher for human baseline.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The test answers will not be publicly released; the authors will maintain an online evaluation platform, refine potential data noise in response to community feedback, maintain the datasets, and evolve the leaderboard in response to new models.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to push AI assistants toward general-purpose capabilities and support development of AI agents for mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The benchmark may have gaps in coverage of certain mathematical problems and visuals; annotations come from heterogeneous original sources and lack unified format; larger numbers of few-shot examples can introduce demonstration bias in some LLM settings.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Coverage may miss some types of mathematical problems and visuals; collecting high-quality data is labor-intensive and scalability/generalizability to other domains remains a concern; only 85.6% of examples have annotations and these annotations are heterogeneous and not unified.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluation of foundation models for mathematical reasoning in visual contexts; testmini is intended for model development validation or limited compute, and test is for standard evaluation.

name.evidence: In this paper, we present M ATHVISTA , a consolidated Math ematical reasoning benchmark in Visual contexts.

description.evidence: To bridge this gap, we present M ATHVISTA , a benchmark designed to combine challenges from diverse mathematical and visual tasks. It consists of 6,141 examples, derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets ( i.e., IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA).

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: It consists of 6,141 examples, derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets ( i.e., IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA). IQTest comprises 228 examples requiring inductive reasoning, abstract thinking, pattem prediction, and calculations, sourced from puzzle test figures on online leaming platforms. PaperQA is a novel dataset featuring questions derived from informative academic illustrations, including tables, figures, and charts from online education resources, with 107 examples sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface1.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Since these datasets are not originally math-targeted, we initially designed heuristic rules to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning from a large pool of candidates. Examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words (as listed in §D.1) in the questions were selected. Each source dataset is limited to up to 400 examples to ensure a balanced representation of each source in our final compiled benchmark. To ensure that each source dataset is well represented in testmini and to maintain a distribution in testmini closely resembling the whole set, we adopted this sampling strategy: (1) first, randomly sample questions with a threshold number of 4 for each source dataset; (2) then, randomly sample the remaining questions for each source dataset on its proportion in the entire set. We also conducted several quality checks to address any unidentified errors.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Therefore, we engaged three expert annotators to manually label these examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning (more details in § D.2). To ensure data quality, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and further refined through a rigorous review process. To ensure consistency in annotation, we employed a two-step process. Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%. To this end, we annotate the examples in M ATHVISTA with information including question type, answer type, language, source, category, task, grade level, and visual context, which can be accurately obtained from the details provided in the source datasets. To verify the quality of automatic annotation, expert annotators manually label the mathematical reasoning categories from seven candidates for 1,000 examples

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: The GUI of the annotation tool is shown in Figure 23 in §D.3. We developed an annotation tool, as illustrated in Figure 22, to enable expert annotators to label problems that involve mathematical reasoning.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Utilizing majority voting and limiting each source dataset to 400 examples, we finalized a collection of 2,739 examples. Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%. Specifically, among the newly collected 736 questions, only 6 exhibited disagreements in the annotated answers. Then, these discrepancies were resolved through discussion among the entire review team, ensuring a consensus was reached on each example. Our analysis yielded a Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775, indicating a substantial level of consistency among the annotators. The results show that 94.1% of the examples from automatic and human annotations have the exact same set of reasoning types, while 98.79% of the individual labels are identical

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Our dataset, M ATHVISTA , is therefore motivated to bridge this gap, offering a robust evaluation benchmark for mathematical reasoning intertwined with visual understanding, thus pushing AI assistants towards general-purpose capabilities. This significant gap underscores the critical role that M ATHVISTA will play in the development of general-purpose AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: One limitation is the dataset coverage. While M ATHVISTA encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks and visual contexts, there may be gaps in the representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. Furthermore, the dataset’s focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts, spanning specific domains like science and college-level math, necessitates a more labor-intensive process for collecting high-quality data compared to textual-only or general-purpose datasets. Thus, the scalability and generalizability of our benchmark to other domains remain a concem. rai:dataUseCases.evidence: Our goal is to conduct both qualitative and quantitative studies to provide a systematic evaluation of existing foundation models for mathematical reasoning capabilities in visual contexts using M ATHVISTA . MATHVISTA consists of 6,141 examples, divided into two subsets: testmini andtest.testmini contains 1,000 examples, intended for model development validation or for those with limited computing resources. The testset features the remaining 5,141 examples for standard evaluation.
